source: DFMMh/FV 466 is of similar size and texture as the other prootics considered here.
evidence: This is a comparative observation.

claim: DFMMh/FV 466+205 are interpreted to belong to the same juvenile individual.
source: Hence, DFMMh/FV 466+205 are herein interpreted to belong to the same juvenile individual.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the articulation and size of the specimens.

claim: DFMMh/FV 561 and DFMMh/FV 964 are left fragmentary prootics containing most of the ASC, the ventral base of the common crus, the anterior ampulla of the LSC, and the anterior base of the lagena.
source: Furthermore, there are two left fragmentary prootics (Figure 7C–F; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, C; DFMMh/FV 561 and DFMMh/FV 964) containing most of the ASC, the ventral base of the common crus, the anterior ampulla of the LSC, and the anterior base of the lagena; both specimens were assigned to relatively mature individuals (Marpmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the specimens, with citation to previous assignment.

claim: DFMMh/FV 561 and DFMMh/FV 964 were assigned to relatively mature individuals.
source: Furthermore, there are two left fragmentary prootics (Figure 7C–F; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, C; DFMMh/FV 561 and DFMMh/FV 964) containing most of the ASC, the ventral base of the common crus, the anterior ampulla of the LSC, and the anterior base of the lagena; both specimens were assigned to relatively mature individuals (Marpmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about previous assignment, supported by citation.

claim: DFMMh/FV 249, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 981.2 are right fragmentary otoccipitals containing at least the posterior parts of the LSC and the lagena, as well as most of their PSCs.
source: The three right fragmentary otoccipitals DFMMh/FV 249, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 981.2 (Figure 8A–F; Figure 8—figure supplements 1A–F and 2A–D) contain at least the posterior parts of the LSC and the lagena, as well as most of their PSCs; these specimens were assigned to immature individuals (Marpmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the specimens, with citation to previous assignment.

claim: DFMMh/FV 249, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 981.2 were assigned to immature individuals.
source: The three right fragmentary otoccipitals DFMMh/FV 249, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 981.2 (Figure 8A–F; Figure 8—figure supplements 1A–F and 2A–D) contain at least the posterior parts of the LSC and the lagena, as well as most of their PSCs; these specimens were assigned to immature individuals (Marpmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about previous assignment, supported by citation.

claim: The morphology of the inner ears contained within the isolated specimens is consistent with what can be observed in DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077.
source: In general, the morphology of the inner ears contained within these isolated specimens is consistent to what can be observed in DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on observation.

claim: Marpmann et al., 2014, used the vascularization (indicated by surface texture) of Europasaurus specimens as a critical character in judging the relative maturity.
source: Since Marpmann et al., 2014, used the vascularization (indicated by surface texture) of Europasaurus specimens as a critical character in judging the relative maturity, the inner cavities surrounding the endosseous labyrinths were examined herein.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in previous research, supported by citation.

claim: No discrete cavities could be found in DFMMh/FV 581.1, DFMMh/FV 1077, DFMMh/FV 964, and DFMMh/FV 561 (all considered to represent more or less mature individuals).
source: No discrete cavities could be found in DFMMh/FV 581.1, DFMMh/FV 1077, DFMMh/FV 964, and DFMMh/FV 561 (all considered to represent more or less mature individuals).
evidence: This is a finding from the examination of the specimens.

claim: The otoccipitals DFMMh/FV 249, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 981.2 and the articulated specimens DFMMh/FV 205 (otoccipital) and DFMMh/FV 466 (prootic) show very similar, or corresponding, patterns of inner cavities.
source: The otocipitals DFMMh/FV 249, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 981.2 and the articulated specimens DFMMh/FV 205 (otoccipital) and DFMMh/FV 466 (prootic) show very similar, or corresponding, patterns of inner cavities (Figures 7 and 8; Figure 7—figure supplement 2; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparative observation, shown in figures.

claim: All four otoccipitals show dorsoventrally deep cavities posterodorsal to anteromedial to the PSC, close to the articulation surface with the supraoccipital.
source: All four otoccipitals show dorsoventrally deep cavities posterodorsal to anteromedial to the PSC, close to the articulation surface with the supraoccipital (except for DFMMh/FV 205, in which this cavity network is not as much extended anteriorly).
evidence: This is a description of the cavities observed in the specimens.

claim: There are T-, V-, or X-shaped (in cross-section in anterior view), dorsoventrally high and mediolaterally thin structures anterior to the PSC and dorsal to the LSC (close to the articulation surface with the prootic) in the otoccipitals.
source: There are T- (DFMMh/FV 898 and DFMMh/FV 981.2), V- (DFMMh/FV 205), or X- (DFMMh/FV 249) shaped (in cross-section in anterior view), dorsoventrally high and mediolaterally thin structures anterior to the PSC and dorsal to the LSC (close to the articulation surface with the prootic).
evidence: This is a description of the cavities observed in the specimens.

claim: All four otoccipital specimens bear relatively small cavities ventral to the LSC (close to the articulation surface with the prootic).
source: Additionally, all four otoccipital specimens bear relatively small cavities ventral to the LSC (again, close to the articulation surface with the prootic).
evidence: This is a description of the cavities observed in the specimens.

claim: DFMMh/FV 981.2 shows dorsoventrally high cavities posteroventrally to the endosseous labyrinth (close to the articulation surface with the basioccipital).
source: DFMMh/FV 981.2 shows dorsoventrally high cavities posteroventrally to the endosseous labyrinth (close to the articulation surface with the basioccipital).
evidence: This is a description of the cavities observed in the specimen.

claim: The cavities of DFMMh/FV 205 seem not as large and extensive as in the other three otoccipitals.
source: Generally, the cavities, likely of vascular purpose, of DFMMh/FV 205 seem not as large and extensive as in the other three otoccipitals.
evidence: This is a comparative observation.

claim: The smaller size and lesser extent of cavities in DFMMh/FV 205 coincides with it being the largest, smoothest and, hence, most mature of the juvenile otoccipitals.
source: This coincides with their size and assumed relative maturity (DFMMh/FV 205 being the largest, smoothest and, hence, most mature of them; see Marpmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation and previous research, supported by citation.

claim: DFMMh/FV 466 bears a small cavity ventral to the LSC (corresponding to the respective cavity in the otoccipital DFMMh/FV 205).
source: Whereas DFMMh/FV 466 bears a small cavity ventral to the LSC (corresponding to the respective cavity in the otocipital DFMMh/FV 205), no other unequivocal cavities could be found, which is surprising when the V-shaped cavity close to the prootic contact of DFMMh/FV 205 is considered.
evidence: This is an observation from the specimen.

claim: No other unequivocal cavities could be found in DFMMh/FV 466, which is surprising when the V-shaped cavity close to the prootic contact of DFMMh/FV 205 is considered.
source: Whereas DFMMh/FV 466 bears a small cavity ventral to the LSC (corresponding to the respective cavity in the otocipital DFMMh/FV 205), no other unequivocal cavities could be found, which is surprising when the V-shaped cavity close to the prootic contact of DFMMh/FV 205 is considered.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation.

claim: The position and morphology of the dorsal expansion of Europasaurus gives a rather 'upright' or sigmoidal appearance to the endocast.
source: Although not as prominent as in Dicraeosaurus (Janensch, 1935; Paulina Carabajal et al., 2018) and some specimens of Diplodocus (Witmer and Ridgely, 2008a), the position and morphology of the dorsal expansion of Europasaurus gives a rather 'upright' or sigmoidal appearance to the endocast (Figure 1A; see also Paulina-Carabajal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative description supported by citations, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The 'upright' or sigmoidal appearance of the Europasaurus endocast is partly explained by the (preservational) lack of its olfactory bulb and tract.
source: This is partly explained by the (preservational) lack of its olfactory bulb and tract.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed morphology.

claim: The first cranial nerve is not expected to be very long in many sauropods, especially in the closely related macronarian taxa Camarasaurus and Giraffatitan.
source: The first cranial nerve is not expected to be very long in many sauropods, especially in the closely related macronarian taxa Camarasaurus and Giraffatitan (Witmer and Ridgely, 2008a; Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009; see also Müller, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claim: The braincase endocast is rather tubular in some taxa, for example, the early-diverging sauropodomorph Buriolestes, the rebbachisaurid Nigersaurus, and the titanosaur specimen MCCM-HUE-1667.
source: In contrast, the braincase endocast is rather tubular in some taxa, for example, the early-diverging sauropodomorph Buriolestes (Müller et al., 2021), the rebbachisaurid Nigersaurus (Sereno et al., 2007), and the titanosaur specimen MCCM-HUE-1667 (Knoll et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: The endocast of Europasaurus seems to be most similar to Giraffatitan.
source: Instead, the endocast of Europasaurus seems to be most similar to Giraffatitan (Janensch, 1935; Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009; formerly Brachiosaurus brancai, see Paul, 1988; Taylor, 2009).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: Contrary to other sauropod taxa, there are no discrete canals for vascular features such as the rostral middle cerebral vein or the orbitocerebral vein on the endocast of Europasaurus.
source: Contrary to other sauropod taxa (e.g., Spinophorosaurus, Diplodocus, Camarasaurus, and Sarmientosaurus; see Witmer et al., 2008b; Knoll et al., 2012; Martínez et al., 2016), there are no discrete canals for vascular features such as, for example, the rostral middle cerebral vein or the orbitocerebral vein on the endocast of Europasaurus.
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: A ventral ridge on the medulla, as seen in Europasaurus, seems to be present, although not as pronounced, in Thecodontosaurus, the early-diverging sauropod specimen OUMNH J13596, Spinophorosaurus, Camarasaurus and, potentially, Giraffatitan.
source: A ventral ridge on the medulla, as seen in Europasaurus (Figures 1A—3A), seems to be present, although not as pronounced, in Thecodontosaurus (Ballell et al., 2021), the early-diverging sauropod specimen OUMNH J13596 (Bronzati et al., 2018), Spinophorosaurus (Knoll et al., 2012), Camarasaurus (Witmer and Ridgely, 2008a) and, potentially, Giraffatitan (Janensch, 1935; Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009) as well.
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations, shown in figures.

claim: Giraffatitan seems to bear a median fossa posteromedially to the proximal CN VI openings.
source: Although not obvious on the endocast (Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009), Giraffatitan seems to bear a median fossa posteromedially to the proximal CN VI openings (Janensch, 1935: Figure 117); the respective protuberance in Europasaurus marks a distinct kink on the endocast (Figures 2C and 3; Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations, shown in figures.

claim: The endocast of Europasaurus bears two pairs of canals on the ventrolateral aspect of the pituitary, the posterior of which is interpreted to represent the internal carotid.
source: The endocast of Europasaurus bears two pairs of canals on the ventrolateral aspect of the pituitary, the posterior of which is interpreted to represent the internal carotid here (Figures 1A—3; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; in accordance with Marpmann et al., 2014: Figure 13A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the endocast, supported by citation, shown in figures.

claim: Structures identified as the craniopharyngeal canal are present anterior to the carotid artery in the titanosaur specimen CCMGE 628/12457 and the diplodocid specimen MMCh-Pv-232 (assigned to Leinkupal).
source: Whereas structures identified as the craniopharyngeal canal are present anterior to the carotid artery in the titanosaur specimen CCMGE 628/12457 (Sues et al., 2015) and the diplodocid specimen MMCh-Pv-232 (assigned to Leinkupal; Garderes et al., 2022), they are situated posteriorly in Apatosaurus (Balanoff et al., 2010; see also Paulina-Carabajal, 2012, and Paulina Carabajal et al., 2014 for subcondylar foramina in the vicinity of the internal carotid arteries).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In Apatosaurus, structures identified as the craniopharyngeal canal are situated posteriorly to the carotid artery.
source: Whereas structures identified as the craniopharyngeal canal are present anterior to the carotid artery in the titanosaur specimen CCMGE 628/12457 (Sues et al., 2015) and the diplodocid specimen MMCh-Pv-232 (assigned to Leinkupal; Garderes et al., 2022), they are situated posteriorly in Apatosaurus (Balanoff et al., 2010; see also Paulina-Carabajal, 2012, and Paulina Carabajal et al., 2014 for subcondylar foramina in the vicinity of the internal carotid arteries).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: In the taxa where the craniopharyngeal canal has been identified, it is a singular median canal.
source: However, in these taxa, the craniopharyngeal canal is a singular median canal.
evidence: This is a comparative observation.

claim: The anterior of the two pairs of canals on the ventral aspect of the pituitary in Europasaurus may be the canals for the neurohypophysis.
source: This may render the anterior of the two pairs of canals on the ventral aspect of the pituitary in Europasaurus the canals for the neurohypophysis (Paulina-Carabajal, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The pituitary of the Europasaurus endocast of DFMMh/FV 581.1 does not project much more ventrally than the posteroventral margin of the medulla oblongata.
source: The pituitary of the Europasaurus endocast of DFMMh/FV 581.1 does not project much more ventrally than the posteroventral margin of the medulla oblongata.
evidence: This is an observation from the endocast.

claim: The pituitary is slightly higher dorsoventrally than the ASC in DFMMh/FV 581.1.
source: The pituitary is slightly higher dorsoventrally than the ASC (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the endocast, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Usually in sauropods, the pituitary is large and inclined posteroventrally, reaching much more ventrally than the ventral margin of the hindbrain.
source: Usually in sauropods, the pituitary is large and inclined posteroventrally, reaching much more ventrally than the ventral margin of the hindbrain (see, e.g., Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009; Martínez et al., 2016; see also Sues et al., 2015 for an extreme reached in the titanosaur specimen CCMGE 628/12457 with a short ASC and an enormous pituitary).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: The finding of a relatively small pituitary fossa in Europasaurus and early-diverging sauropodomorphs seem to support a close connection of body and pituitary size.
source: The finding of a relatively small pituitary fossa in Europasaurus and early-diverging sauropodomorphs seem to support a close connection of body and pituitary size, as suggested by some authors (Nopcsa, 1917; Edinger, 1942; Müller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The microCT data of DFMMh/FV 581.1 suggest that the right CN VI canal closely passes by the pituitary fossa without a penetration.
source: The microCT data of DFMMh/FV 581.1 suggest that the right CN VI canal closely passes by the pituitary fossa without a penetration, whereas the left CN VI canal tangents on the pituitary fossa and opens into the latter (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the microCT data, shown in figure.

claim: The left CN VI canal tangents on the pituitary fossa and opens into the latter in DFMMh/FV 581.1.
source: The microCT data of DFMMh/FV 581.1 suggest that the right CN VI canal closely passes by the pituitary fossa without a penetration, whereas the left CN VI canal tangents on the pituitary fossa and opens into the latter (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the microCT data, shown in figure.

claim: The feature of the CN VI canals not penetrating the pituitary fossa seems typical for titanosaurs.
source: The feature of the CN VI canals not penetrating the pituitary fossa seems typical for titanosaurs (e.g., Paulina-Carabajal, 2012; Knoll et al., 2015; Paulina-Carabajal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009 note a penetration or connection of CN VI canals on the endocast MB.R.1919 of Giraffatitan.
source: Whereas Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009 note such a penetration or connection on the endocast MB.R.1919, Janensch, 1935, originally described penetrating canals in the Giraffatitan braincase specimens S 66 (on which the endocast MB.R.1919 is based) and Y 1.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Janensch, 1935, originally described penetrating CN VI canals in the Giraffatitan braincase specimens S 66 and Y 1.
source: Whereas Knoll and Schwarz-Wings, 2009 note such a penetration or connection on the endocast MB.R.1919, Janensch, 1935, originally described penetrating canals in the Giraffatitan braincase specimens S 66 (on which the endocast MB.R.1919 is based) and Y 1.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research, supported by citation.

claim: The Giraffatitan braincase specimen t 1 seems to show CN VI canals rather passing by the pituitary fossa.
source: However, the Giraffatitan braincase specimen t 1 seems to show CN VI canals rather passing by the pituitary fossa (Janensch, 1935).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research, supported by citation.

claim: The variation in CN VI canal penetration of the pituitary fossa may suggest a certain role of individual expressions, asymmetries, and/or represents a phylogenetically potentially reasonable intermediate state.
source: This may suggest a certain role of individual expressions (Giraffatitan), asymmetries (Europasaurus), and/or represents a phylogenetically potentially reasonable intermediate state (nonetheless, this feature may also be prone to preservational bias).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observations.

claim: The endosseous labyrinth of Europasaurus is most similar to Giraffatitan and Spinophorosaurus in bearing a relatively long ASC and a long lagena.
source: The endosseous labyrinth of Europasaurus (Figure 6) is most similar to Giraffatitan (Janensch, 1935) and Spinophorosaurus (Knoll et al., 2012) in bearing a relatively long ASC and a long lagena.
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In dorsal view, the anterior ampulla of the short LSC in Europasaurus displays a medially concave gap between the ASC and LSC.
source: In dorsal view, the anterior ampulla of the short LSC in Europasaurus displays a medially concave gap between the ASC and LSC (Figure 6B,F,J).
evidence: This is a description of the morphology, shown in Figure 6.

claim: A pronounced concavity is present between the LSC and the PSC in Europasaurus (best seen in dorsal view).
source: Similarly, a pronounced concavity is present between the LSC and the PSC (best seen in dorsal view).
evidence: This is a description of the morphology.

claim: Both concave gaps (the ASC and the PSC project further laterally than the lateral outline of the LSC reaches medially) are similarly present in many Titanosauriformes.
source: Both concave gaps (the ASC and the PSC project further laterally than the lateral outline of the LSC reaches medially) are similarly present in many Titanosauriformes (with the exception of FAM 03.064; Knoll et al., 2019): Giraffatitan (Janensch, 1935), Malawisaurus (Andrzejewski et al., 2019), Sarmientosaurus (Martínez et al., 2016), CCMGE 628/12457 (Sues et al., 2015), Jainosaurus (Andrzejewski et al., 2019), Ampelosaurus (Knoll et al., 2013), Narambuenatitan (Paulina-Carabajal et al., 2020), Bonatitan, Antarctosaurus, MCF-PVPH 765 and MGPIFD-GR 118 (Paulina-Carabajal, 2012), but also in the rebbachisaurids Limaysaurus and Nigersaurus (Paulina-Carabajal and Calvo, 2021).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: The lagena of Europasaurus is conspicuously thick mediolaterally, especially when compared to its anteroposterior slenderness.
source: Although the mediolateral width of the lagena does not appear to be associated with auditory capabilities (Walsh et al., 2009), the lagena of Europasaurus is conspicuously thick mediolaterally, especially when compared to its anteroposterior slenderness (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a description of the morphology, with citation for context, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The calculated auditory capacities impute Europasaurus a relatively wide hearing range with a high upper frequency limit (among non-avian dinosaurs).
source: The calculated auditory capacities (based on Walsh et al., 2009) impute Europasaurus a relatively wide hearing range with a high upper frequency limit (among non-avian dinosaurs; Lautenschlager et al., 2012; King et al., 2020; Sakagami and Kawabe, 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on calculations, supported by citations.

claim: Walsh et al., 2009, demonstrate a certain correlation between hearing range, complexity of vocalization, and aggregational behaviour in extant reptiles and birds.
source: Walsh et al., 2009, demonstrate a certain correlation between hearing range, complexity of vocalization, and aggregational behaviour in extant reptiles and birds (see also Gleich et al., 2005; Hanson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research, supported by citations.

claim: It appears plausible that Europasaurus lived in groups with conspecifics, which made airborne communication crucial.
source: Following their conclusions and other studies suggesting (age-segregated) gregariousness in sauropodomorphs on the basis of nesting sites, body, and ichnofossils (e.g., Lockley et al., 2002; Sander et al., 2008; Myers and Fiorillo, 2009; Pol et al., 2021a), it appears plausible that Europasaurus lived in groups with conspecifics (although it is not clear whether this took place perennial or seasonal, e.g., for 'brooding'), which made airborne communication crucial.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the auditory capabilities and comparative studies, supported by citations.

claim: Taphonomic reasons suggest at least 21 individuals of Europasaurus in close temporal and spatial connection with very young and very old individuals being rarely represented.
source: Furthermore, taphonomic reasons (femora count suggests at least 21 individuals in close temporal and spatial connection with very young and very old individuals being rarely represented; Scheil et al., 2018) and evidence for two morphotypes in the cranial and postcranial material of Europasaurus may suggest some form of social cohesion (Carballido and Sander, 2013; Marpmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about taphonomic evidence, supported by citation.

claim: Evidence for two morphotypes in the cranial and postcranial material of Europasaurus may suggest some form of social cohesion.
source: Furthermore, taphonomic reasons (femora count suggests at least 21 individuals in close temporal and spatial connection with very young and very old individuals being rarely represented; Scheil et al., 2018) and evidence for two morphotypes in the cranial and postcranial material of Europasaurus may suggest some form of social cohesion (Carballido and Sander, 2013; Marpmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: While a given species is likely to perceive sounds within the frequency spectrum it is able to produce, it may be rather unlikely that the full range of frequencies that can be heard is covered by the sound production ability.
source: However, while a given species is likely to perceive sounds within the frequency spectrum it is able to produce, it may be rather unlikely that the full range of frequencies that can be heard is covered by the sound production ability (see also Walsh et al., 2009; Senter, 2008).
evidence: This is a general statement about auditory capabilities, supported by citations.

claim: 'Acoustically cluttered' habitats like forests seem associated with a tendency towards high-frequency intraspecific communication in recent mammals.
source: Habitat preferences potentially play a role as well: 'acoustically cluttered' habitats like forests seem associated with a tendency towards high-frequency intraspecific communication in recent mammals (Charlton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about habitat and communication, supported by citation.

claim: Tropic Late Jurassic conditions in Europe may be part of the explanation of the recovered auditory capacities of Europasaurus.
source: Together with tropic Late Jurassic conditions in Europe (Armstrong et al., 2016), this may be part of the explanation of the recovered auditory capacities of Europasaurus.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Marpmann et al., 2014 considered the prootic DFMMh/FV 466 more mature than the otoccipital DFMMh/FV 205.
source: An interesting issue are the different morphological ontogenetic stages of DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 mentioned in Marpmann et al., 2014. The authors considered the prootic DFMMh/FV 466 more mature than the otoccipital DFMMh/FV 205.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research, supported by citation.

claim: DFMMh/FV 466 is about as large as the prootics of DFMMh/FV 581.1, DFMMh/FV 1077, DFMMh/FV 964, and DFMMh/FV 561.
source: Indeed, DFMMh/FV 466 is about as large as the prootics of DFMMh/FV 581.1, DFMMh/FV 1077, DFMMh/FV 964, and DFMMh/FV 561 (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but the otoccipital DFMMh/FV 205 is much smaller than the ones in DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 (and only slightly larger than DFMMh/FV 981.2, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 249; Figure 8; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative observation, shown in figures.

claim: The otoccipital DFMMh/FV 205 is much smaller than the ones in DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077.
source: Indeed, DFMMh/FV 466 is about as large as the prootics of DFMMh/FV 581.1, DFMMh/FV 1077, DFMMh/FV 964, and DFMMh/FV 561 (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but the otoccipital DFMMh/FV 205 is much smaller than the ones in DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 (and only slightly larger than DFMMh/FV 981.2, DFMMh/FV 898, and DFMMh/FV 249; Figure 8; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative observation, shown in figures.

claim: The findings support the use of bone surface smoothness as an indicator of vascularization and maturity.
source: In addition to general size of the specimens, and build and rugosity of articular facets, Marpmann et al., 2014 (see also Benton et al., 2010) defined the morphological ontogenetic stages also by bone surface smoothness, advocating for vascularization: the smoother the surface, the lesser the degree of vascularization and – in tendency – the more mature the individual bone. Our findings support this (Figures 7 and 8; Figure 7—figure supplement 2; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the findings supporting previous methods, with citations, shown in figures.

claim: The deep penetration of the cavities into the bone is unambiguous.
source: While the bases of individual cavities described herein may represent depressions of articulation areas, their deep penetration into the bone is unambiguous.
evidence: This is a statement about the observation of the cavities.

claim: The described structures might represent sutures, but the position and orientation of individual cavities do not conform to what would be expected.
source: Apart from this, the described structures might represent sutures. However, the position and orientation of individual cavities do not conform to what would be expected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cavities.

claim: The cavities make sense in the frame of morphological ontogenetic stages used in Marpmann et al., 2014, and are considered as so far unknown vascular expressions of juvenile Europasaurus individuals.
source: Since these cavities make sense in the frame of morphological ontogenetic stages used in Marpmann et al., 2014, they are considered as so far unknown vascular expressions of juvenile Europasaurus individuals here.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cavities, supported by citation.

claim: DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 articulate very well with each other, especially on their lateral aspects.
source: DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 articulate very well with each other, especially on their lateral aspects.
evidence: This is an observation from the specimens.

claim: There are cavities ventral to the LSC in DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 that seem to have been continuous originally.
source: Additionally, there are cavities ventral to the LSC that seem to have been continuous originally (Figure 5; Figure 7A, B; Figure 8G, H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the specimens, shown in figures.

claim: In DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077, the fenestra ovalis is considerably smaller than the vagal foramen.
source: However, whereas the fenestra ovalis is considerably smaller than the vagal foramen in DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 (Figure 3B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), it seems that in DFMMh/FV 466+205 this is vice versa (although this impression may be due to the fragmentary nature of the latter two specimens; Figure 5L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a comparative observation, shown in figures.

claim: In DFMMh/FV 466+205, the fenestra ovalis seems larger than the vagal foramen (although this impression may be due to the fragmentary nature of the specimens).
source: However, whereas the fenestra ovalis is considerably smaller than the vagal foramen in DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 (Figure 3B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), it seems that in DFMMh/FV 466+205 this is vice versa (although this impression may be due to the fragmentary nature of the latter two specimens; Figure 5L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a comparative observation with caution, shown in figures.

claim: If DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 are in articulation, there is a large gap on their common dorsal aspect.
source: If DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 are in articulation, there is a large gap on their common dorsal aspect (Figure 5J; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is an observation from the specimens, shown in figures.

claim: Considering DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 and the braincase of Massospondylus, the supraoccipital usually occupies the gap on the dorsal aspect between the prootic and otoccipital.
source: Considering DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 and, for example, the braincase of Massospondylus (Chapelle and Choiniere, 2018), the supraoccipital usually occupies this gap.
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citation.

claim: The preserved parts of the conjoined endosseous labyrinth of DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 displays the same general features as DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 and is anteroposteriorly almost as long as the latter two specimens.
source: In case our interpretation of a common bond between DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 is misleading and they actually represent two differently matured individuals, it is still noticeable that the preserved parts of the conjoined endosseous labyrinth of DFMMh/FV 466 and DFMMh/FV 205 displays the same general features as DFMMh/FV 581.1 and DFMMh/FV 1077 and is anteroposteriorly almost as long as the latter two specimens (Figures 5 and 6; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a comparative observation, shown in figures.

claim: The observation suggests an allometric growth between the prootic and otoccipital: during growth, the prootic reaches the 'adult' size faster than the otoccipital.
source: This suggests an allometric growth between the prootic and otoccipital: during growth, the prootic reaches the 'adult' size faster than the otoccipital, producing a surprisingly small paroccipital process (or a surprisingly large prootic) in juvenile individuals of Europasaurus (seemingly, also seen in Massospondylus; Sues et al., 2004), containing a relatively large endosseous labyrinth (see also Fabbri et al., 2021, for ontogenetic transformations in the cranium of sauropodomorphs).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observations, supported by citations.

claim: A relatively large immature endosseous labyrinth seems also to be present in the ornithischians Dysalotosaurus, Psitaccosaurus, and Triceratops.
source: A relatively large immature endosseous labyrinth seems also to be present in the ornithischians Dysalotosaurus (Lautenschlager and Hübner, 2013), Psitaccosaurus (Bullar et al., 2019), and Triceratops (Morhardt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: The endosseous labyrinth appears relatively large in juveniles of Massospondylus and the extant, precocial ostrich.
source: Furthermore, the endosseous labyrinth appears relatively large in juveniles of Massospondylus (Neenan et al., 2019) and the extant, precocial ostrich (Romick, 2013), and stays morphologically relatively stable throughout ontogeny (see also Jeffery and Spoor, 2004).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: The vestibular apparatus detects movements with the aid of endolymphatic fluid and cilia contained within the semicircular canals, which is crucial for locomotion.
source: The vestibular apparatus detects movements with the aid of endolymphatic fluid and cilia contained within the semicircular canals, which is crucial for locomotion (see, e.g., Benson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the function of the vestibular apparatus, supported by citation.

claim: A relatively large and morphologically adult-like endosseous labyrinth in expectedly very young individuals of Europasaurus suggests that hatchlings had to be light on their feet very fast in this dwarfed sauropod taxon.
source: Thus, a relatively large and morphologically adult-like endosseous labyrinth in expectedly very young individuals of Europasaurus suggests that hatchlings had to be light on their feet very fast in this dwarfed sauropod taxon.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation of the endosseous labyrinth.

claim: Europasaurus has a rather sigmoid general braincase endocast shape, with a comparably large dorsal expansion, two openings for CN XII, an angle of 50° between the pituitary fossa and the LSC, and the ASC is clearly dorsoventrally higher than the PSC.
source: Europasaurus has a rather sigmoid general braincase endocast shape, with a comparably large dorsal expansion, two openings for CN XII, an angle of 50° between the pituitary fossa and the LSC, and the ASC is clearly dorsoventrally higher than the PSC (Figures 1—4 and Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings, shown in figures.

claim: The findings add to the knowledge about dinosaur neuroanatomy.
source: This and additional novel details, such as the highly uniform vascular cavities within the juvenile braincase material (Figures 7 and 8; Figure 7—figure supplement 2; Figure 8—figure supplement 2), add to our knowledge about dinosaur neuroanatomy.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the study, shown in figures.

claim: The relatively small pituitary fossa in an insular dwarf lends support to the old idea of being a proxy for body size.
source: The relatively small pituitary fossa (Figure 1A) in an insular dwarf lends support to the old idea of being a proxy for body size (Nopcsa, 1917; Edinger, 1942; Müller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Many sauropods were extremely large land-dwellers as adults, and still, started as tiny hatchlings, indicating enormously fast growth rates.
source: Many sauropods were extremely large land-dwellers as adults, and still, started as tiny hatchlings, indicating enormously fast growth rates (e.g., Carpenter, 1999; Hallett and Wedel, 2016; Curry Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about sauropod biology, supported by citations.

claim: The threat arising from the discrepancy of several tens of tons between adults and juveniles makes it unlikely that sauropods were able to take good care for their offspring.
source: The threat arising from the discrepancy of several tens of tons between adults and juveniles makes it, among other reasons, unlikely that these animals were able to take good care for their offspring (e.g., Sander et al., 2011; Curry Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The size discrepancy between adults and juveniles implies a great mobility early in life (precociality in a broader sense) of sauropods.
source: This implies a great mobility early in life (precociality in a broader sense; see Dial, 2003; Iwaniuk and Nelson, 2003) of sauropods (Sander et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Europasaurus seemingly retained characteristics potentially associated with precociality from its large-bodied ancestors.
source: Although Europasaurus represents an island dwarf (adults were probably not as dangerous for their juveniles), having roamed islands not exceeding an area of three times modern-day Bavaria (Sander et al., 2006), this taxon seemingly retained characteristics potentially associated with precociality (and therefore potentially r-strategy; Sander et al., 2008; Myers and Fiorillo, 2009; Hallett and Wedel, 2016) from its large-bodied ancestors.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Europasaurus individuals likely stayed in a certain social cohesion, and potentially practiced colonial nesting as is known from other sauropodomorphs.
source: As also suggested by the taphonomic circumstances (Sander et al., 2006; Carballido and Sander, 2013; Marpmann et al., 2014; Scheil et al., 2018; see also Supplementary file 1), Europasaurus individuals likely stayed in a certain social cohesion, and potentially practiced colonial nesting as is known from other sauropodomorphs (Lockley et al., 2002; Sander et al., 2008; Myers and Fiorillo, 2009; Pol et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The findings add hints towards the nature of aggregation with a certain complexity of reproductive and social behaviours for Europasaurus.
source: In concert with the approximate auditory capabilities offered here, our findings add hints towards the nature of aggregation with a certain complexity of reproductive and social behaviours for these little real-life titans, thriving in Europe some 154 Ma ago.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings.

claim: The articulated braincase specimen of E. holgeri, DFMMh/FV 581.1, together with both loose parietals (DFMMh/FV 581.2 and 3), is traversed by breakages but not strongly deformed.
source: The articulated braincase specimen of E. holgeri, DFMMh/FV 581.1, together with both loose parietals (DFMMh/FV 581.2 and 3), is traversed by breakages but not strongly deformed, lacking parts of the anterior and dorsomedial skull roof, as well as the anteromedial walls of the endocranial cavity.
evidence: This is a description of the preservation of the specimen.

claim: The articulated and assembled braincase lacks the frontals, the right orbitosphenoid and laterosphenoid.
source: The articulated and assembled braincase lacks the frontals, the right orbitosphenoid and laterosphenoid.
evidence: This is a description of the preservation of the specimen.

claim: The parietals are anteriorly, posterodorsomedially, and posteriorly incomplete and somewhat deformed.
source: The parietals are anteriorly, posterodorsomedially, and posteriorly incomplete and somewhat deformed (if they fit posteromedially with the supraoccipital they do not fit with the supraoccipital, prootic and laterosphenoid further anteriorly, and vice versa).
evidence: This is a description of the preservation of the specimen.

claim: The braincase of the macronarian G. brancai suggests a plain posterior skull roof not exceeding the dorsal extent of the sagittal nuchal crest; this served as an orientation for reconstructing the Europasaurus braincase.
source: The braincase of, for example, the macronarian G. brancai suggests a plain posterior skull roof not exceeding the dorsal extent of the sagittal nuchal crest; this served as an orientation here.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the study.

claim: MicroCT of DFMMh/FV 581.1, 2, and 3 was performed using a Metrotom 1500 in a subsidiary of Zeiss in Essingen.
source: MicroCT of DFMMh/FV 581.1, 2, and 3 (Figures 1—3; Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4) was performed using a Metrotom 1500 (Carl Zeiss Microscopy GmbH, Jena, Germany) in a subsidiary of Zeiss in Essingen; 1804 images were recorded with binning 1 resulting in a DICOM data set (for further details of settings and voxel size, see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: All other specimens were documented with a Xradia MicroXCT-200 of the Imaging Center of the Department of Biology, University of Greifswald.
source: All other specimens (Figures 4, 5, 7 and 8; Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2; Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2) were documented with a Xradia MicroXCT-200 (Carl Zeiss Microscopy GmbH, Jena, Germany) of the Imaging Center of the Department of Biology, University of Greifswald; 1600 projection images were recorded each, using 0.39× objective lens, with binning 2 (for further details of settings and voxel size for each specimen, see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: Digital segmentation and measurements were produced utilizing the software Amira (5.6).
source: Digital segmentation and measurements were produced utilizing the software Amira (5.6), based on DICOM files (DFMMh/FV 581.1, 2, and 3) and tiff files (remaining material).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: The microCT data were manually segmented to create 3D surface models.
source: The microCT data were manually segmented to create 3D surface models.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: In DFMMh/FV 581.1, 2, and 3, the X-ray absorption of the fossil and the sediment within is quite similar, resulting in low contrast in many places.
source: In DFMMh/FV 581.1, 2, and 3, the X-ray absorption of the fossil and the sediment within is quite similar, resulting in low contrast in many places.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the data.

claim: For preservational reasons, the extent of the digital model of the endocast was conservatively estimated on the skull roof and on the anterodorsal region.
source: Furthermore, for preservational reasons (lack of both frontals, right orbitosphenoid, laterosphenoid, and loose parietals), the extent of the digital model of the endocast was conservatively estimated on the skull roof and on the anterodorsal region; some asymmetries on the endocast are explained by this circumstance.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods and limitations of the study.
